<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>PostgreSQL 19's "scary patch contest"</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1092003/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1092003/</guid>
			<dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
			<description><p><a href="https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/19.0/">PostgreSQL 19</a> was 
expected to be released in September, in keeping with the database
project's longstanding tradition of a major release every year. However,
some late-breaking concerns about several of the features slated for inclusion
has some developers worried about the quality of the release. On August 25, PostgreSQL
contributor Robert Haas <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/CA+Tgmob9NY6m0YNFTQ4nFH2d0iC9SQRruDYxfndGKKzh8OC80w@mail.gmail.com/">sent
an email</a> with the subject "<q>scary patch contest</q>" about several patches
that have required an unusually large number of bug fixes leading up to the
release, which has raised questions about their readiness for a stable
release. One of the patches has been reverted, but several are still under heavy
revision, and an extra beta release has been slotted in to allow for additional
testing.</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 24 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Accelerating the kernel's build process</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1093398/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1093398/</guid>
			<dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
			<description>Kernel developers do a lot of kernel builds.  Since the kernel is not a
small program, those builds can take a fair amount of time, even on a fast
machine.  The kernel also has a complex build system; it is probably fair
to say that few developers truly understand it, and fewer still are willing
to try to improve it.  Lorenzo Stoakes, armed with LLM-based assistance,
decided to give it a try, though, and has managed to reduce the time it
takes to build a kernel — and not by a small amount.
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 24 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Lessons learned as the Debian Project Leader</title>

			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1093381/</guid>
			<dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
			<description><p>What is it like to be a Debian Project Leader (DPL), or a former one?
According to Andreas Tille, who stepped down this year after two consecutive
terms as DPL, you'd have to be one to know. At the recent <a

the initiatives he led, mistakes that he made, and his thoughts on the <a
href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1087134/">general resolution (GR) on large
language model (LLM) usage in Debian</a>.</p>
</description>

		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Adding BPF to blk-iocost</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1093661/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1093661/</guid>
			<dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
			<description>The scheduling of block <span class="nobreak">I/O</span> requests has long
been a challenge for operating-system kernels.  For many years, the
performance characteristics of rotating drives meant that putting
considerable resources into request ordering was worthwhile.  In a world
with fast, solid-state drives, scheduling is more concerned with enforcing
fairness between competing users while being fast enough to keep up with
drives that can perform millions of <span class="nobreak">I/O</span>
operations per second.  The blk-iocost <span class="nobreak">I/O</span>
controller was designed for the solid-state world and generally performs
well, but there is always a desire to do better.  <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20260914073356.791518-1-cui.tao@linux.dev">This patch
series</a> from Tao Cui aims to make blk-iocost more flexible by enabling
the loading of a BPF program to make cost decisions.
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 24 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Ways to encrypt data on servers</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1092553/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1092553/</guid>
			<dc:creator>jake</dc:creator>
			<description>At the <a href="https://2026.fossy.ca/">2026 edition of FOSSY</a>, Romeo
Solano gave a fast-paced, humorous presentation on what could have been a
rather boring topic: server encryption.  There are a number of threats that
we face in today's world, from criminals, government overreach, espionage,
and more, that can be thwarted with encryption.  But encrypting data on a
system that may live elsewhere, without any access to its keyboard at boot
time, is rather more difficult than encrypting the disk of a laptop.
Solano described the problems and gave a tour of some of the solutions in
the talk.
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 24 Sep 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Thread-identity switcheroo for io_uring</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1094303/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1094303/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>The <a
href="https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/io_uring.7.html">io_uring
subsystem</a> is all about asynchronous execution; applications count on it
to not block — unless explicitly requested to.  Within io_uring, maintaining
the "never blocks" guarantee has sometimes been a challenge, given that
many paths in the kernel were never designed for asynchronous execution.
This problem has been worked around, but at a significant cost to
performance.  Now, io_uring maintainer Jens Axboe has posted <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20260911154148.644489-1-axboe@kernel.dk">an RFC patch set</a>
with a somewhat radical (and potentially scary) solution to the problem.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 01 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Testing compat_linux on NetBSD with the Linux Test Project</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1094310/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1094310/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p><a href="https://netbsd.org/">NetBSD</a> has long had support for
running Linux binaries via its kernel-level <a
href="https://man.netbsd.org/compat_linux.8"><tt>compat_linux</tt></a>
feature, but test coverage for it was less complete than some might
hope. In order to provide better testing for <tt>compat_linux</tt>,
Google Summer of Code (GSoC) participant Henrique Brito opted to work
on enabling the <a
href="https://linux-test-project.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Linux Test
Project (LTP)</a> test suite to compile and run on NetBSD. At <a
href="https://2026.eurobsdcon.org/">EuroBSDCon&#160;2026</a>, Brito's
mentor, Stephen Borrill, provided a report on the project, and the
status of LTP on NetBSD. The work has already resulted in some minor
fixes, and a good list of additional problems to solve.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 01 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">

        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Pierre-Emmanuel Patry and Arthur Cohen gave a talk at
<a href="https://rustconf.com/">
RustConf&#160;2026</a> on the
status of the Rust frontend for GCC (gccrs), with a particular eye toward the
goal of
<a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1083202/">
compiling the Linux kernel</a>. Patry gave a follow-up talk for a more
kernel-focused audience at
<a href="https://kangrejos.com/">
Kangrejos</a> the next week, which Cohen could not attend. The
<a href="https://rust-gcc.github.io/">
gccrs project</a> is
making good progress overall, but it will still be some time until the compiler
is usable.
</p>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Ideas on modernizing the open-source desktop</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095425/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095425/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>Scott Jenson has been working on user interfaces (UIs) and user experience (UX)
for many years at Apple, Google, and other companies. Now, he's trying to convince
open-source projects to experiment more and drive the desktop beyond the age-old "<a
href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WIMP_(computing)">windows, icons, menus,
pointer</a>" (WIMP) model. At <a
href="https://akademy.kde.org/2026/">Akademy&#160;2026</a>, KDE's annual developer
conference, he shared his complaints and ideas in a talk aimed
at convincing those in attendance to take the lead on desktop design.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 01 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Listening to the radio with Rust</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095721/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095721/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Many of the transmissions sent over the radio spectrum can
be decoded with a relatively cheap hardware dongle. Thomas Eckert presented at
<a href="https://rustconf.com/">
RustConf 2026</a> in Montreal about his hobby:
decoding radio transmissions with Rust.
In his presentation, he
covered all of the math necessary to get started with
<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software-defined_radio">
software-defined radio</a>,
and gave demonstrations of listening to AM and FM radio, as well as decoding
transmissions from
aircraft transponders. His slides and example code are
<a href="https://github.com/t-eckert/listening-to-the-radio-with-rust#listening-to-the-radio-with-rust">
available</a> on GitHub.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 08 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">

        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>The <a href="https://www.sovereign.tech/">Sovereign Tech Agency</a> (STA) is
<a href="https://www.sovereign.tech/tech/kde">investing nearly â‚¬1.3 million</a>
